claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
GeoDeploy is an open source example (released as open source at the time of the post) built by pairing TypeSafe's Jev with the Pulumi Automation API.
GeoDeploy uses Jev to pick the best AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud region for the user's users, gates every AI decision on confidence, and provisions Kubernetes via Pulumi.
GeoDeploy prices/compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes.
GeoDeploy asks Jev to pick the best region per geo from a closed list, so Jev cannot hallucinate a region.
GeoDeploy gates every Jev decision on confidence, with hard rejects for data residency.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent clusters using one Pulumi stack per region.
GeoDeploy scales itself in self-driving mode, with a human in the loop (suggestion for approval) when Jev's confidence is low.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, which it describes as its SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's AI primitives are 'powerful'.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no ('noul') questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are 'the perfect complement to agentic work'.
GeoDeploy takes a deployment request (target geos, image, workload shape, constraints), decides where the container image should run and what it will cost, and then builds the answer.

A GeoDeploy deployment request has four parts: target geos (locations, traffic share per place, and a data-residency rule of EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image (container image and platforms amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max number of providers, budget).
GeoDeploy picks the best region for each geo and provisions consistent environments across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, does all the math, and never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, and never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS, and never decides anything.
GeoDeploy normalizes each business region (geo) to a canonical location and residency class.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as its coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, and normalizes them into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy uses plain, deterministic TypeScript to bin-pack pods onto nodes, filter out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and compute a monthly cost per candidate region.
Jev picks the winning region and modules for each geo in GeoDeploy's decide step.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules covering EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy's provisioning step will not run unless the user's cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The link '/automation/' points to an existing Pulumi Automation API page on pulumi.com.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a `plan.json` and `plan.md` containing the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Unlike a general-purpose LLM, Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence.
Jev exposes three primitives: `choice()`, `score()`, and `noul()`.
Jev's `choice()` primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's `score()` primitive rates something against a rubric the user describes; GeoDeploy's rubrics use 10 levels.
Jev's `noul()` primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.

GeoDeploy only lets Jev select from closed sets (region IDs GeoDeploy has already priced and checked); Jev never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region like `us-west-9` or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

In its single per-geo call, GeoDeploy asks Jev for a selection (`choice`), five quality scores (`score`: coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (`noul`: data residency satisfied, enough capacity), and a fallback region (`choice`).
The GeoDeploy repository contains the file `packages/decide/src/questions.ts` with a `buildStageAQuestions` function that builds the Jev questions.
The `@typesafe-ai/sdk` package exports `choice`, `noul`, and `score`.

The `@typesafe-ai/sdk` `TypeSafeClient` has a `systemOne({ state, questions })` method that returns a result with an `answers` object, exposing `a.selection.choice`, `a.selection.confidence`, `a.residencyOk.noul`, and `a.coverage.score`.
The options passed to `choice()` are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
TypeSafe's advice for writing rubrics is to 'describe situations, not degrees.'

GeoDeploy's rubrics have 10 levels, each a concrete scenario, running from 'Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence' up to 'In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center.'
GeoDeploy sends the whole Jev question set in one call, along with the state Jev reasons over.
GeoDeploy's five Jev scores feed a ranking system that runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's ranking weights live in code, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy's weight profiles are: latency-optimized {cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12}; balanced {0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.12, 0.18}; residency-first {0.12, 0.12, 0.38, 0.23, 0.15}; failure-domain {0.08, 0.17, 0.48, 0.15, 0.12}.
GeoDeploy's composite ranking score subtracts the sprawl-risk score (weighted) rather than adding it, because extra cloud providers mean more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.

In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), so Jev is only asked about ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.
GeoDeploy checks every Jev answer against a confidence threshold matched to how risky the decision is.
GeoDeploy's data-residency confidence threshold is 0.95, and failing it causes a hard reject.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for choosing a region for a new cluster is 0.90; if it doesn't pass, the top three candidates are flagged for a human to choose.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for choosing a region when a stack already exists is 0.75; if it doesn't pass, the existing region is kept.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for an ingress or autoscaling module choice is 0.85; if it doesn't pass, the registry default is used.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for the node-pool sizing tier is 0.60; if it doesn't pass, the bin-packing result is used.
GeoDeploy has a global confidence floor of 0.50 for region pick, residency, or capacity answers; below it, the AI path is dropped for that geo.

The residency check shown is from `packages/decide/src/engine.ts` in the GeoDeploy repository, and enforcing a confidence gate is plain deterministic code, followed by validation that the selection is one of the candidates.
Each `AiPathAborted` error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

When a GeoDeploy gate check fails, the Jev API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
Running `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.
When self-driving mode is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`, the GeoDeploy agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization.

In self-driving mode, GeoDeploy asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options `no-change`, `scale-up:<geo>`, `scale-down:<geo>`, or `shift:<from>-><to>`, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In self-driving mode, code (not Jev) computes the actual node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, GeoDeploy applies the resize automatically above 0.85 Jev confidence, suggests it for human approval between 0.70 and 0.85, and below 0.70 ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.

CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric; once a traffic baseline is established it is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency, error rates, or application-specific metrics.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy, and anyone with access to Jev and a cloud provider can get started.
The GitHub repository pulumi/devx-geodeploy exists and hosts GeoDeploy.
The page /docs/iac/automation-api/ exists on pulumi.com as the Pulumi Automation API docs.
https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction is TypeSafe's Jev documentation.
Pulumi's X account is @PulumiCorp at https://x.com/PulumiCorp.
Pulumi offers a free account that can be signed up for at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
